frontend.prompt:
Scope (decided from requirement): detail endpoints for individual items (GET, PUT, DELETE) and the list endpoint; client cache/state; optimistic updates; UI messages and tests. Do not change owner/superuser privileges or list semantics.

Acceptance contract (must be implemented exactly):
- When a regular (non-owner, non-superuser) user performs GET, PUT, or DELETE on another user's existing item, the client must receive HTTP 404 with JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"}.
- When a requested item ID does not exist, the client must receive the same HTTP 404 and identical JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"}.
- Successful responses for owners and superusers must remain unchanged.
- The list endpoint continues to return only items visible to the current user; client list behavior need not change.

Frontend implementation instructions:
1) Error handling for item detail requests (GET/PUT/DELETE):
   - Treat any response with HTTP status 404 and body JSON.detail === "Item not found" as a canonical "not found" case. Do not present any server-provided resource attributes to the user in this case.
   - UI behavior for that case: show a consistent "Not found" / "Item not found" message in place of the resource view or editing form. Do not show reasons like "no permission" or any other distinguishing text that reveals whether the item existed.
   - For PUT/DELETE if the client used optimistic updates, rollback the optimistic change on receiving the 404 and show the same not-found message.

2) Cache/state management:
   - If the client caches item detail (local store, client-side DB, in-memory), remove or mark the item as not present when receiving the 404 described above. Do not leave or surface cached attributes that might belong to other users.
   - When rolling back optimistic updates because of this 404, do not expose server error detail beyond the canonical not-found message.

3) Request/response checks (implementation detail):
   - When handling responses, check both status === 404 and parsedBody.detail === "Item not found" before applying the not-found logic. If status === 404 but body differs, treat as generic error (log and show a generic error message) — do not assume any other body shape.
   - For any non-404 error (5xx, 401, 403, 400, etc.) keep existing error handling, except: do not transform other error statuses into the canonical 404 behavior.

4) UX wording & disclosure:
   - Message presented to users must not reveal whether the item existed or whether access was denied; use neutral wording: e.g., "Item not found" or "This item could not be found." Keep wording consistent with the backend detail string where appropriate, but do not reveal backend internals.
   - Do not populate forms or previews with any attributes returned in the 404 response (the backend will not include attributes, but ensure client code does not leak stale cache entries when this 404 is encountered).

5) Logging & telemetry (frontend):
   - Log metadata (endpoint, HTTP method, status, user action) for debugging, but never log or send item attribute values to logs/telemetry when the response was the canonical 404.

6) Tests to add/adjust (integration & unit):
   - Test: owner GET returns success and displays data.
   - Test: superuser GET returns success and displays data.
   - Test: other user GET returns HTTP 404 with body {"detail":"Item not found"}, UI shows not-found message and no item data.
   - Tests for PUT/DELETE with owner (success behavior unchanged).
   - Tests for PUT/DELETE with other user: simulate server returning 404 with the exact body; verify optimistic updates are reverted and UI shows not-found message and no resource info.
   - Test: requesting a non-existent item ID returns the same 404 body and the UI behavior is identical to the unauthorized-other-user case.
   - Test: list page continues to show only visible items (existing list tests should cover this); ensure no cross-user items are shown.

7) Non-assumptions / contract boundaries (do not change or assume):
   - Do not assume or change the format of successful responses for owners/superusers.
   - Do not assume the endpoint path or authentication mechanism; adapt checks to the existing client routing and auth token mechanisms in your app.

Deliverables for frontend work:
- Code changes implementing the error handling and cache/state adjustments described above.
- Automated tests listed in section 6.
- Short QA checklist describing how to verify: owner user sees items; other user gets 404 and UI shows not-found; caches are cleaned; optimistic updates are rolled back on 404.

Notes for implementer:
- Use exact string match to "Item not found" in the response JSON.detail when choosing the canonical not-found flow.
- If your client framework or http library returns non-parsed bodies on 404, ensure parsing is attempted safely and fallback to generic error handling if parsing fails.

backend.prompt:
Scope (decided from requirement): item detail endpoints (GET, PUT, DELETE) and item list endpoint. Authentication and permission checks as currently available must be used. Do not change owner and superuser privileges or successful response formats for them. Ensure identical response for "missing" and "unauthorized-other-user" cases for detail endpoints.

Acceptance contract (must be implemented exactly):
- For regular (non-owner, non-superuser) users who attempt GET, PUT, or DELETE on another user's existing item, the API must return HTTP 404 with JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"}.
- For requests for item IDs that do not exist, the API must return the same HTTP 404 and identical JSON body {"detail": "Item not found"}.
- Owners and superusers retain their existing successful behaviors and response shapes; do not change those.
- The list endpoint must continue to only return items visible to the current user. No change to list semantics except to ensure no accidental leaks.

Backend implementation instructions:
1) Request handling for item detail endpoints (GET/PUT/DELETE):
   - On a request to an item detail endpoint, perform authorization checks using existing auth context (e.g., request.user). Determine ownership (is_owner(user, item)) and superuser status (is_superuser(user)).
   - Behavior flow:
     a) Attempt to fetch the item by ID when needed for the operation. If the item is not found, return HTTP 404 with JSON body exactly {"detail": "Item not found"}.
     b) If the item is found but current user is neither the owner nor a superuser, return HTTP 404 with JSON body exactly {"detail": "Item not found"}.
     c) If the user is the owner or a superuser, proceed with the normal operation and return the same success responses as before.
   - Important: for (a) and (b) the response must be byte-for-byte identical in HTTP status and JSON body so clients cannot distinguish missing vs. unauthorized-other-user.

2) Response details:
   - Use HTTP status 404 and Content-Type: application/json. Body must be a JSON object with a single field: {"detail": "Item not found"}. Do not add other keys in these 404 responses (no codes, no hints, no debug info).
   - Do not convert other existing error responses (e.g., 401, 403, 400, 500) to this 404; only the two cases above must use the canonical 404.

3) List endpoint:
   - Ensure list queries are filtered to only include items the current user is allowed to see (existing behavior per requirement). Do not include items owned by other users unless existing rules already allow it for the requesting user type (owner/superuser). No additional side channels should leak other users' items.

4) Logging and monitoring:
   - Internally log unauthorized access attempts for auditing (e.g., attempted access by user X to item ID Y). However, logs must not be returned in responses.
   - Rate-limit or batch repetitive unauthorized logging to avoid enabling enumeration via log timing or volume.

5) Tests to add/adjust (unit and integration):
   - Test: owner GET returns success (no change to current response) and payload contains expected attributes.
   - Test: superuser GET returns success (no change).
   - Test: other user GET for existing item returns 404 with exact body {"detail": "Item not found"}.
   - Test: GET for non-existent item ID returns 404 with exact same body.
   - Repeat tests for PUT and DELETE: owner/superuser success unchanged; other user and non-existent item both return identical 404 and body.
   - Test list endpoint returns only visible items for current user.
   - Tests must assert exact HTTP status and JSON body match for the canonical 404 case.

6) Implementation guidance / safe patterns:
   - Fetch-then-check: fetch item by ID; if not found => return canonical 404; if found => check ownership/superuser; if unauthorized => return canonical 404.
   - Be careful not to return 403 for unauthorized-other-user. The requirement is explicit: return 404 instead.
   - Do not include item details in 404 responses under any circumstance.

7) Backwards compatibility and non-assumptions:
   - Do not alter successful response schemas for owners and superusers.
   - Do not assume any particular field names beyond the required response detail in the 404 case.
   - Do not change list endpoint contract beyond ensuring it filters visible items.

8) Deployment and verification checklist:
   - Deploy code to a staging environment and run the tests in section 5.
   - Manual verification: as owner -> view/modify/delete works; as other user -> requests for the same resource return 404 JSON exactly; requesting a nonexistent ID returns same 404 JSON.

9) Security note:
   - The canonical 404 is intended to avoid information leakage about resource existence. Ensure middleware and error handlers do not override or enrich the 404 body in the canonical cases.

Deliverables for backend work:
- Code changes implementing the fetch/permission-check flow and canonical 404 responses.
- Automated unit and integration tests listed above that assert exact status and body.
- Short QA checklist for staging verification.

Do not make any other contract changes. If there are endpoint naming, authentication, or serialization details not covered by this prompt, integrate these instructions into your app's existing request/response patterns without changing the required 404 behavior or owner/superuser success behavior.
